title: Duck Confit
subtitle: Slow-cooked duck legs cured and preserved in their own fat
excerpt: Duck legs cured overnight in salt and herbs, then submerged in duck fat and cooked at a very low temperature until the meat is silky and falling from the bone. Finished with a blast of high heat to crisp the skin.

recipe.sourceNotes: Confit (from the French confire, to preserve) is one of the oldest methods of food preservation, dating back to medieval France and found particularly in the Gascony region of southwest France. Duck confit (confit de canard) is the most famous application of the technique: duck legs are cured in salt and herbs, then cooked very slowly submerged in their own rendered fat, which acts as a cooking medium and, once set, as a barrier to oxygen that preserved the meat for months without refrigeration. Today the preservation aspect is rarely the motivation; the technique is valued for the extraordinary texture it produces: meat that is deeply flavoured, silky, and tender in a way that no other cooking method replicates. Confited legs can be refrigerated submerged in their fat for up to one month.

recipeTools.notes: A deep baking dish that holds the duck legs snugly.

content.text: The cure draws moisture from the surface of the duck and seasons the flesh deeply. Pat the legs completely dry after curing: any remaining moisture will cause the fat to spit during cooking. The fat must barely bubble during cooking: the target temperature is 90 C. At this temperature, the collagen in the leg converts to gelatine over the long cooking period, producing the characteristic silky texture. To finish: place the confited legs skin-side up in a very hot oven (220 C) or under a hot grill for 10 to 15 minutes until the skin crackles and blisters.

items.preparation: from a tin; enough to submerge the legs

content.text: Mix together the salt, crushed garlic, thyme, bay, and pepper. Rub all over the duck legs. Place in a dish, cover, and refrigerate for 12 to 24 hours. Remove from the fridge 30 minutes before cooking. Pat the legs completely dry with kitchen paper.

Heat the oven to 140 C / fan 120 C / gas 1. Melt the duck fat in a small saucepan. Arrange the duck legs in a snug baking dish. Pour over the melted fat: the legs should be submerged or close to it. Cover tightly with foil. Cook for 2 hours 30 minutes until the meat is very tender and beginning to pull away from the bone.

Lift the legs out of the fat. To serve now: place skin-side up on a baking tray and roast at 220 C / fan 200 C / gas 7 for 12 to 15 minutes until the skin is crackled and golden. Serve with lentils, sautéed potatoes, or a simple green salad.
